body:
This doesn't appear to match https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-subresource-integrity/#the-integrity-attribute, in particular it disallows the option expressions and disallows multiple integrity values.

I think the processing model of just passing the string to Fetch most naturally works by supporting those.

So I think we can eliminate this definition and instead say that it must match the `integrity-metadata` production.

Furthermore, we should make sure there are some basic smoke tests of these exciting other forms of integrity metadata, to make sure they work. E.g. `blah-asdf sha256-realhash` should work, with the `blah-asdf` getting ignored; cases with lots of extra whitespace on either side should work fine; and you should be able to do things like `sha256-realhash?!-!!@-#-あ` and that should not cause problems (per https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-subresource-integrity/#parse-metadata).

body:
There are three concepts here:

- URL strings. This includes things like `"https://example.com/"`, `"./a.js"`, and `"a.js"`.

- Module specifiers. This includes the same three types of strings, but the meaning of `"a.js"` is different: it's a bare specifier and thus can only be given meaning via an import map.

- URL-like module specifiers. These only include `"https://example.com/"` and `"./a.js"`. `"a.js"` is not included.

`import()` requires module specifiers, not URLs. So without an import map, you're seeing that error.

The point I'm raising here is that the `"integrity": {}` JSON map is _conceptually_ a map from URLs to integrity values. (Not a map from module specifiers to integrity values.) However, you've _syntactically_ restricted it to URL-like module specifiers.

This is probably good. It's equivalent to restricting it to a subset of URL strings that are unambiguous. But it's unusual for the web platform.

---

The test to write is the following. Add a bogus integrity hash for `"a.mjs"` (no leading `./`). Then do `import("./a.mjs")`. The import should be allowed.

This test would fail if the keys of the import map were being interpreted as URLs. Then, `"a.mjs"` would be equivalent to `./a.mjs`. But since the spec text has decided to only parse as URL-like module specifiers, `"a.mjs"` is just a parsing error.
